To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Piper species that differ in chemical defenses are more likely to co-occur than expected by chance and 2) Piper species are, on average, phylogenetically closer than expected by chance in local communities, but there is no phylogenetic structure for chemical composition.

(1) co-occurring Piper species differ in secondary chemistry more than expected by chance; (2) there is no phylogenetic relationship between Piper species in terms of secondary chemical composition; and (3) species in local communities are more closely related than expected at random, suggesting that functional trait differences other than those measured in this study are important for assembly.

1) coexisting Piper species have more divergent chemical defenses than expected by chance; 2) Piper phylogenetic relatedness is not related to chemical divergence, suggesting that other functional traits also influence local assembly; 3) Piper species in local communities are, on average, less phylogenetically divergent than expected by chance.

the mechanisms that facilitate the coexistence of hyper-diverse plant species.

plant chemical diversity is important for community structure, but the role of chemical diversity is likely to be mediated by other ecological processes.
